fatal_errors: The proposed 600–800 °C aging intervention does not reconstruct the relevant 1100–1300 °C annealing and water-quenching comparison.
It treats chemical short-range order and resolvable B2 ordered precipitates as essentially the same mediator, without distinguishing local SRO from long-range ordering and phase separation.
It omits the central cooling pathway: BCC miscibility-gap spinodal decomposition into reciprocal Ni–Al-rich and Co–Cr–Fe-rich products, followed by B2 ordering.
The assumed rapidly quenched, minimally ordered random-solid-solution baseline is not established for this alloy and may still decompose or order during quenching.
Claims concerning radiation tolerance, corrosion resistance, and cryogenic toughness are not supported by the cited evidence.
explanation: The hypothesis addresses the broad design problem and offers a controlled, measurable comparison, but it is not a reconstruction of the target study. Its limited point of agreement is that Ni–Al-associated B2 ordering within a disordered matrix can obstruct dislocations. It misses the specified Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 alloy, high-temperature annealing series, reciprocal hierarchical BCC/B2 morphology, FCC-temperature trend, sequential spinodal decomposition, and monotonic hardness increase from about 39 to 50 HRC. The experiment could discriminate whether aging-induced ordering correlates with several properties, although varying aging time also changes precipitate size, fraction, segregation, and matrix composition, so it does not isolate SRO. Evidence E1 supports useful strength and ductility in a compositionally different lamellar FCC/B2 eutectic alloy, while E2 supports SRO-related dislocation strengthening only in simulated MoNbTaW; neither validates the proposed radiation, environmental, or cryogenic benefits. The falsification rule is also overly conjunctive: failure of any one claimed co-benefit would reject a broad hypothesis even if the proposed strengthening mechanism were correct.
